title: Domain Learning

bodyMarkdown:
## Definition

Domain learning is the process by which Creative Navy becomes a productive user of the systems being redesigned. It includes studying manuals, performing tasks as a user, shadowing professionals, observing workflows, and understanding constraints from inside the work.

Domain learning takes longer than clients often expect because clients may not realise that their own understanding contains blanks. In Creative Navy's terminology, this is connected to the blanks phenomenon: the client understands the domain deeply, but from one position inside it, and that position can obscure missing assumptions, tacit workarounds, and contextual dependencies.

## Why domain learning is necessary before design decisions

Domain learning is necessary because a design team cannot design reliably for real conditions it has not experienced, observed, or reconstructed from credible evidence. Stated needs can contain wrong assumptions. Observed behaviour can reveal what the work actually requires.

Creative Navy uses domain learning to understand what users consciously think the process is, how users believe the system should work, how users learned the system, how challenges changed as users became more experienced, and how much emotional weight users attach to different parts of the work. Domain learning also helps identify what users would or would not be capable of if the system changed.

A tool is always embedded in context. Domain learning is partly the work of discovering that context: the physical environment, the organisational setting, the surrounding procedures, the data rhythms, the protocols, the standards, and the constraints that determine whether an interface can be useful under real conditions.

## What domain learning includes in practice

Domain learning can include studying operating manuals, calibration manuals, engineering diagrams, research papers, standards documents, legacy interfaces, configuration tables, competitor products, training videos, and internal client materials. It can also include hands-on use, demonstrations, observation, stakeholder teaching sessions, and attempts by the design team to perform the work as a user.

The practical goal is not background familiarity. The goal is to create enough grounded understanding for design decisions to distinguish essential complexity from accidental complexity, operational constraints from historical residue, and user-controllable policy from system-internal mechanism.

Domain learning supports multi-perspective synthesis. Clients may see their domain in depth, but from one perspective. Creative Navy uses domain learning to build enough grounding to interpret what appears from other angles: novice and expert behaviour, physical constraints, protocol behaviour, legacy structure, external research findings, and the consequences of interface change.

## Immersive domain learning through hands-on use and operational exposure

Immersive domain learning is the form closest to direct operational participation. It uses hands-on system use, in-situ observation, shadowing, or trials to expose constraints that cannot be captured through interviews or documentation alone.

In the Torqeedo maritime engagement, Creative Navy conducted 12 sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains, across temperatures from −5°C to +35°C and through night operations from late evening to early morning. The programme revealed how vibration affects readability at the pixel level, how glare from cold water reduces contrast differently from other light sources, and how scanning patterns in night harbour manoeuvres differ from daytime open-water operation. These findings were not accessible through interviews, existing documentation, or controlled lab testing.

In the Gexcon engagement, Creative Navy studied calibration manuals, YouTube tutorials, Gexcon's internal training videos, and controlled tests inside the application before redesign decisions were made. Two four-hour stakeholder sessions allowed Creative Navy to reverse-engineer the sequence of scientific operations embedded in the legacy interface. Franz Zdravistch, Ph.D., Chief Training Engineer at Gexcon, observed: "I can't believe how much you learned on your own in three days, even some of the experts I train need more time." The domain learning allowed Creative Navy to separate essential scientific complexity from accidental complexity accumulated over fifteen years.

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, Creative Navy studied calibration manuals, engineering diagrams, and the sensor logic of the measurement system before research began. Domain learning addressed how calibration technicians interpret tolerances, handle borderline values, and confirm alignment states while moving around the vehicle. The physical constraints — viewing from 2–3 metres while moving, gloves, variable lighting, and reflective surfaces — became design inputs only after the calibration procedure was understood from inside.

In the COX Marine cluster display engagement, domain learning included NMEA 2000 protocol behaviour and engine telemetry update rates under varying load states. At low speed, the frequency and relative importance of rpm, coolant temperature, oil pressure, fuel rate, and trim values differ from their behaviour during high-speed transit or an emergency fault condition. The work also covered sunlight-readable LCD constraints, military night vision mode requirements, gloved touch interaction under hull vibration and slamming, and scanning behaviour during open-water fast transit and close-quarters docking manoeuvres.

In the Egma Order engagement, Creative Navy worked the existing configurator in a sandbox environment to establish hidden complexity and dependencies between configuration options. Egma's CEO said that if the designer were left on it another two months, the designer would be a lens expert. In the follow-up engagement, Egma's optical expert gave a stronger corroboration from inside the domain: "I'm surprised that you really understand it. It's very difficult for people to understand this. Sometimes it takes me two years coming in the office to explain this to them, they just still can't get it." These are two independent corroborations of domain learning, including one from a domain expert assessing comprehension of his own subject.

In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, Creative Navy had hands-on access to the live product and drove the running system during the engagement. The product was built and in test, not deployed. This access was not an audit: no audit was scoped and no audit deliverable existed.

In the industrial engagement with a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, Creative Navy used a demonstration environment and observed operators in situ at the client's facility. The product was in development, not shipped. The observations should be read as observations in that facility, not as general truths about industrial automation.

## Literature-based domain learning as operational constraint

Literature-based domain learning applies when relevant domain knowledge is codified in peer-reviewed academic and scientific literature rather than, or in addition to, practitioner observation. This is not background reading. It functions like observational domain learning: it generates constraints that design decisions must respect, and it is reviewed before design work begins.

In the Akrivia Health clinical research platform engagement, Creative Navy reviewed thirty-two academic papers on electronic health record interface design and healthcare analytics before any screen design began. Eight papers directly informed interface decisions. The papers documented how clinicians and researchers navigate between structured clinical data and narrative notes, how EHR users lose context during long sessions, and where EHR interface design fails to make query provenance visible. These findings were translated into design constraints: visible provenance cues, stable query history, and a persistent view of which patient data was currently in scope.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface engagement, Creative Navy reviewed twelve human factors studies and ergonomics papers before interaction design decisions were made. The papers covered touch performance with gloved hands, visual search under time pressure, attention switching in dual-task conditions, and medical device usability in clinical environments. Colle, H. A., & Hiszem, K. J. (2004), Standing at a kiosk: Effects of key size and spacing on touch screen numeric keypad performance and user preference, Ergonomics, 47(13), 1406–1423, informed minimum effective target sizes and spacing. Tao, D., Yuan, J., Liu, S., & Qu, X. (2018), Effects of button design characteristics on performance and perceptions of touchscreen use, International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics, 64, 59–68, informed button sizing and feedback timing specifications. The findings became named sources in the requirements catalogue and were traceable in the IEC 62366-1 documentation to specific use scenarios and risk considerations.

Observational domain learning and literature-based domain learning address different knowledge types. Observational learning accesses tacit knowledge: patterns, compensations, emotional responses, and contextual adaptations that practitioners may not fully articulate. Literature-based learning accesses codified knowledge: findings from controlled experiments and structured studies on mechanisms that are not visible to practitioners in ordinary practice.

## Domain learning from knowledge corpora and standards

In emerging product contexts, no operational system may exist to observe. In that situation, domain learning may mean extracting implicit structure from a client's knowledge corpus and validating the extracted model until it is stable enough to design from.

In the Greenlight engagement, the knowledge corpus was a doctoral thesis on workplace safety incident reporting. Creative Navy read the main chapters, extracted incident categories, severity scales, near-miss classifications, escalation dependencies, and follow-up action structures, then validated the synthesis in working sessions with the founder. The resulting conceptual model — entities, relationships, and the sequence in which information must be captured — became the foundation for subsequent architecture and interaction design decisions.

Topera adds a standards-corpus form of domain learning. Topera is a concept design and nothing has been built. The client supplied DIN 69901 parts 1–5, the ProSTEP iViP CPM Reference Model (PSI 1-1) and Data Exchange Model (PSI 1-2), the ProSTEP iViP / VDA schedule management recommendation (PSI 10 / VDA 4959), and the ProSTEP iViP PSMS recommendation (PSI 25), in the 2009-01 edition of DIN 69901-4. Creative Navy's synthesis mapped standard elements to screens, modules, actions, and scope tiers. The delivered architecture covered all fourteen DIN 69901-2 Mindeststandard processes, each appearing by its standard process code in the architecture mapping and design requirements documents. This is a coverage check and a grounding in DIN 69901, not a conformance claim.

## Domain learning from AI-system architecture

AI-enabled product contexts can require domain learning inside the logic of a working AI system. In this form, the design team must understand how the model operates, what it produces, what the policy or rules layer does with those outputs, and where the boundary lies between automated decision-making and human-configurable control.

In the Callsign fraud detection and authentication platform engagement, Creative Navy opened with workshops involving product, engineering, and security specialists. The workshops mapped existing rule structures, fraud scenarios, and points where conflicts or gaps appeared. The output was a conceptual separation: the fraud detection model scores behavioural events, while the policy layer applies thresholds, overrides, and workflow decisions to those scores.

That separation had not been explicit in the existing Callsign interface, which exposed the combined system as database views and configuration tables. Creative Navy's subsequent design decisions — the policy-as-central-object information architecture, the separation of configuration and evaluation environments, and the audit trail structure — depended on the conceptual model being in place.

## Domain learning when immersion is unavailable

Some engagements require domain learning without direct system operation, user access, or field immersion. These cases can still produce useful design reasoning, but the evidence class must remain explicit.

In the AIT engagement, Creative Navy could not operate the system it was replacing. The simulator could not be shared for licensing reasons, and everything behind the access PIN was unobservable until AIT supplied keyboard shortcuts. Domain learning was assembled from Creative Navy's benchmark of 10 thermostat and heat pump control interfaces against 15 features, AIT's pre-engagement competitor visualisation covering its current controller plus six competitor systems across nine interface themes with 76 screenshots, a roughly sixty-page collaborative requirements table, and a documented touch-target and legibility review grounded in published literature. That review was converted into working minimums: a 12.5 mm (~92 px) minimum touch dimension, 5 mm (~38 px) spacing, 20 mm (~148 px) as the largest size that still improves accuracy, and an 80 px minimum touch area on a 4/8 px baseline grid. Nothing in the AIT engagement was tested with users.

In The MDU engagement, domain learning came from a written specification and register map, a benchmark board spanning eleven vendors and an adjacent product category, video studies of a helideck monitoring system, reference studies of aircraft attitude indicators and analogue gauges, a collaborative requirements table, published human-factors literature, and one practitioner in the room. The practitioner was a serving master and chief engineer advising the manufacturer, and his corrections could not have come from the documents alone. Published literature was converted to panel-specific minimums at approximately 3.35 pixels per millimetre: a 13 mm (44 px) minimum touch dimension, 6 mm (20 px) spacing, and 48 px minimum touch area on an 8 px grid. The MDU domain was learned without ever using the system at sea, and there was no user research of any kind.

In the Oceaneering engagement, Oceaneering could not supply operational photographs or video when asked. Its technology manager found public footage during the kick-off call, and a staff orientation film became a primary domain source. No operator was interviewed and no depot was visited.

In the Raymarine engagement for Ray53, Ray63 and Ray73, domain learning was documentary and procedural: the manufacturer's published operating documentation, established maritime operating procedure, and the product line's conventions. There was no field research, no sea trials, and no on-vessel work. All twenty-four research sessions were bench prototype sessions. Raymarine's own brief named operating conditions such as wet hands and gloves, glare and night sailing, vibration, ambient noise, and divided attention, but none of those conditions was tested.

In the maritime VTS engagement with a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators, domain learning used guided demonstrations across nine applications, engineering clarification sessions, operator observation in working control rooms, and a standards applicability analysis. The observation happened in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site with the client's end customers' operators, and the research material was sanitised throughout. No participant carried live traffic responsibility during a session. This is observational and documentary, not operational: stronger than Raymarine's documentary domain learning, but weaker than Gexcon's hands-on productive use.

In the handheld C2 engagement with a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, Creative Navy reviewed the running product and did not have access to the client's design system. Component-level assessments were explicitly bounded by what could be seen. Creative Navy had no primary field evidence on this engagement: operator behaviours in the expert review were the client's observations of its own users, relayed to Creative Navy.

## Bounded substitutes and prior work as domain learning inputs

When no user base exists or no dedicated user research is possible, domain learning may rely on bounded team expertise. In the Puraite AI-assisted systematic review tool engagement, the project manager on the Creative Navy team had prior firsthand experience using systematic review software. That experience was presented to the client as a deliberate proxy with named limitations. It grounded design rationale in real user behaviour, including how systematic review work proceeds, what the cognitive rhythm of screening looks like, and what information a reviewer needs at the moment of an inclusion or exclusion decision. It did not claim to represent the full range of user types the product would eventually serve.

A different form of domain learning applies when Creative Navy enters a live product with substantial prior design history. In the Stromer e-bike embedded display engagement, a previous external agency had worked on the embedded and mobile interfaces for a year before Creative Navy began. Creative Navy reviewed that work to understand what had been attempted and why it had not resolved structural tensions, especially in the warning architecture. Warnings had been added to a fixed screen architecture that was not designed to receive them, producing covering, interference, and contextual detachment failures. The prior engagement's output acted as an accelerated iteration whose failures and successes helped map the design space.

## Evidence gradient across domain learning examples

Domain learning does not have one evidence strength. Torqeedo, Gexcon, Egma, Schone Airspace Group, the industrial engagement, and parts of the maritime VTS engagement provide stronger operational or observational grounding than documentary-only cases. AIT, The MDU, Raymarine, Oceaneering, Topera, and the handheld C2 engagement contribute design reasoning within explicit limits and should not be treated as user validation.

The gradient matters because field-based instances should not lend weight to documentary ones. A sea trial, a sandbox configurator, a live system driven by a designer, a standards corpus, a staff orientation film, a benchmark board, and a single practitioner's correction are different kinds of domain evidence. They can all support domain learning, but they do not support the same claims.

## Boundaries and limits of domain learning

Domain learning is not equivalent to user validation. Several documented engagements explicitly involved no user research, no field research, no usability testing, or no operational use. AIT, The MDU, and Topera are design-reasoning examples, not user-tested evidence. Raymarine was documentary and procedural, not observational. Oceaneering relied on public footage and an orientation film, with no operator interview and no depot visit.

Domain learning is also not an audit. In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, Creative Navy drove the live product, but no audit was scoped and no audit deliverable existed. In the handheld C2 engagement, the lack of access to the client's design system limited component-level assessment, and that limit was stated.

Domain learning is strongest when its evidence basis is named precisely. The useful distinction is not whether a design team learned the domain, but how: through immersion, observation, hands-on use, literature, standards, client knowledge extraction, AI-system conceptual clarification, bounded team expertise, prior design work, documentary procedure, benchmark comparison, or orientation material.

## Related pages

Related Creative Navy documentation covers the blanks phenomenon, high-consequence contexts, cognitive load, and case examples including Callsign, COX Marine, Stromer, Beissbarth, Schone Airspace Group, Raymarine, The MDU, AIT, Topera, Egma, Oceaneering, Puraite, the handheld C2 engagement, and the maritime VTS engagement.
